'''Cherlynlavaughn Bradley''' (October 27, 1951 – August 30, 2014) was an American [[chemist]] who worked at [[Amoco]].

== Early life and education ==
Bradley was born in [[Chicago|Chicago, Illinois]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=whhnDwAAQBAJ&dq=cherlynlavaughn+bradley&pg=PT373|title=African American Women Chemists in the Modern Era|last=Brown|first=Jeannette E.|date=2018-08-08|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=9780190615192|language=en}}</ref> Her father, Leroy Bradley, worked at [[Burlington Railroad]] and her mother, Geneva Bradley, was a musician.<ref name=":0" /> Bradley attended St Matthew's Catholic School and became interested in science when she was given a Gilbert Chemistry set.<ref name=":0" /> She took a course in [[Advanced Placement|advanced placement]] chemistry and went on to study chemistry and [[Illinois Wesleyan University]].<ref name=":0" /> She was the only African-American student and graduated [[magna cum laude]] in 1973, and went on to study inorganic chemistry at graduate school.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/annualcommenceme1975nort|title=Annual commencement / Northwestern University.|last=Northwestern University (Evanston|first=Ill )|date=1975|publisher=Evanston, Ill. : The University|others=Northwestern University}}</ref> At [[Northwestern University]], Bradley was, again, the only African-American woman in the department. She worked on polymer semiconductors and linear permethylpolysilanes.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://chicagoacs.org/images/downloads/Chemical_Bulletin/14oct.pdf|title=THE CHICAGO SECTION MOURNS THE LOSS OF CHEMICAL BULLETIN EDITOR CHERLYNLAVAUGHN BRADLEY|date=2014|website=ACS|access-date=2018-09-14}}</ref> She earned her PhD in 1978.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://www.northwestern.edu/magazine/spring2015/alumnilife/passings.html|title=Passings: Northwestern Magazine - Northwestern University|website=www.northwestern.edu|access-date=2018-09-14}}</ref>

== Research and career ==
Bradley joined [[Standard Oil]] in 1977, which later became [[Amoco]].<ref name=":0" /> She worked on elemental detection for sulfur compounds. She was nominated to join the [[American Society for Testing and Materials]] and led the gas chromatography study group.<ref name=":0" /> The group included [[Amoco]], [[Royal Dutch Shell]], [[Chevron Corporation]], [[Mobil]] and [[Marathon Oil]].<ref name=":0" /> She was likely the only African-American woman with a PhD to work at [[Amoco]], and made efforts to mentor young women.<ref name=":0" />

She developed a [[Microwave plasma]] [[gas chromatography]] detector that could detect trace elements.<ref name=":0" /> She worked with [[Hewlett-Packard]] to develop a small version of the equipment.<ref name=":0" /> She was recognised for her ability to determine polymer contaminants. She was a member of the [[American Chemical Society]]'s [[Project SEED]], an organisation that brought students from economically disadvantaged background to [[Amoco]] for the summer.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> She mentored girls for the [[Girl Scouts of the USA]] chemistry award.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> Bradley was a member of the [[American Chemical Society]]'s Women Chemists committee.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scribd.com/document/102549460/Women-Chemists-Committee-News-Fall-12|title=Women Chemists Committee News Fall '12 {{!}} Mentorship {{!}} Inquiry Based Learning|website=Scribd|language=en|access-date=2018-09-14}}</ref> She died after a short illness on August 30, 2014.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.iwu.edu/news/2014/clips/?page=8|title=Titans in the News {{!}} Illinois Wesleyan|website=www.iwu.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-09-14}}</ref>
